classification_signals: The paper describes a controlled laboratory experiment with human subjects (eight young adults, eight older subjects).
It investigates the effect of manipulated environmental conditions (steady-state vs. temperature drift) on physiological, subjective, and performance outcomes.
It employs quantitative measurements (skin/core temperature, thermal sensation scales, performance tasks) and statistical analyses (ANOVA, linear mixed effects model, stepwise linear regression).
The paper includes 'Methods', 'Results', and 'Discussion' sections, typical of empirical research.
Figures and tables present experimental data and statistical results (e.g., Table 2, Table 3, Figure 4, Figure 6, Figure 10).
title: Differences between young adults and elderly in thermal comfort, productivity, and thermal physiology in response to a moderate temperature drift and a steady-state condition.

limitations: The elderly subjects were healthy, normotensive, and not taking medications that might alter cardiovascular or thermoregulatory responses, which may limit generalizability to the broader elderly population who often use medication.

The differences in thermal physiology and thermal comfort between the majority of the elderly population and young adults might be larger than reported in this study due to the selection of healthy elderly subjects.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated differences between young adults (22-25 years) and elderly subjects (67-73 years) in thermal comfort, productivity, and thermal physiology under a moderate temperature drift (17–25°C, ±2 K/h) and a steady-state condition (21.5°C). Key findings indicate that elderly subjects generally reported lower thermal sensation (by ~0.5 scale units) and felt less comfortable than young adults, preferring a warmer temperature in steady-state conditions. Physiologically, the elderly showed more distal vasoconstriction and lower mean skin and core temperatures. While aging significantly negatively impacted performance (elderly completed 15-20% fewer additions and 5% fewer correct additions), temperature changes or drifts did not affect productivity for either group. The PMV model predicted thermal sensation well for young adults but overestimated it for the elderly by 0.5 scale units. Limitations include the selection of healthy elderly subjects, which may limit the generalizability of physiological and comfort findings to the broader, potentially medicated, elderly population.
